scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance dates to the 17th century and is generally considered an English country dance, though it likely stems from the pre-Christian Irish Rinnce Fada and Scottish Highland reels.
It evolved from the English dance 'Sir Roger de Coverley,' which was brought to Virginia by colonists.
In America, it reached its zenith of popularity between 1830 and 1890, appearing at prestigious events like the governor's inauguration balls in Hartford, Connecticut.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The Virginia reel serves as a social mixer and a display of communal coordination.
Historically, it was a way for different generations to mingle, with the presence of elders providing 'steadiness' to the merriment.
It remains a traditional celebratory dance in American folk circles and a rite of passage for Finnish secondary students.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers form two lines of 5-8 couples facing each other.
The 'head' lady and 'foot' man perform figures (forward and back, two-hand turn, do-si-do), followed by the head man and foot lady.
The head couple then 'reels' down the line: they swing each other by the right arm, then swing the next person in the opposite line by the left arm.
Watch for The Reel, Do-si-do.

Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Two facing lines (longways set); movement occurs in the 'aisle' between lines and behind the lines during the march

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music consists of lively old-time reel music, typically in 2/4 time.

Common tunes include 'Durang's Hornpipe,' 'Old Zip Coon' (Turkey in the Straw), and 'Haste to the Wedding.' In specific modern traditions, such as at the University of Virginia, 'The Rattlin' Bog' or 'Scotland the Brave' are used.
Listen for the Fiddle, Banjo, Piano, Flute.
The pulse is 2/4 at about 110 beats a minute.
A driving, upbeat fiddle-led sound characterized by rapid-fire melodic lines and a steady, percussive accompaniment that emphasizes the 'bounce' of the dance.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Historically performed in ballrooms and community halls, the dance was a 'beautiful expression of refined jollity.' In the 19th century, it was associated with formal attire at inauguration balls.
In modern Finland, it is performed by students in formal evening wear during the 'Vanhojen tanssit' proms.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The dance is historically linked to the fictional character Sir Roger de Coverley.
In American history, it was noted as a favorite at the Hartford governor's inauguration balls, attended by state dignitaries.
Regional variations exist across America, though all share the core 'reel' figure.

The dance is a direct descendant of the English 'Sir Roger de Coverley' and the Irish 'Rinnce Fada.' It is a member of the contra dance or country dance family, sharing structural similarities with the 'Money Musk' and 'Scottish country dances.'
